column3: Near-parallel sequence: wrongdoing, later repentance and repair, then forgiveness and mercy.
Adds that deeds remain attributable in a record, giving the recovery sequence an accountability horizon.
Shows that divine turning can follow an adverse outcome, so the aftermath is not final closure.
Parallels a post-trial course of striving and patience followed by forgiveness and mercy.
Supplies the calf-making wrongdoing from the immediately preceding narrative.
Legal kinship limits and its closing mercy formula do not clarify the focus recovery sequence.
Adds reform after repentance as a parallel condition for forgiveness and mercy.
Shows Moses' return and anger within the calf episode that frames the focus.
Adds a believing group's collective plea for forgiveness and mercy.
Links faith and righteous deeds with the covering of evil deeds and repaired condition.
Continues the same episode with Moses seeking forgiveness and mercy for the people.
Boundary evidence: belief is tested by the force of the preceding discourse, not merely asserted afterward.
Adds that return from a wrongful statement requires a concrete corrective act.
Adds hope for forgiveness at judgment, without the focus's recovery sequence.
Adds a before-and-after ordeal in the Exodus setting and tests conduct after relief.
Sets recompense for evil deeds as a boundary against treating forgiveness as denial of wrongdoing.
Shows the calf-makers recognizing error and pleading for mercy and forgiveness immediately before the focus.
Presents faith and righteous action as joined, supporting faith as enacted rather than merely claimed.
Keeps punishment and forgiveness together in Israel's later history, preserving a non-final judgment horizon.
Provides Moses' direct prayer for forgiveness and entry into mercy within the same episode.
Boundary evidence: disbelief can void deeds, contrasting the focus's believing reorientation.
Adds a sustained progression of guarding, faith, and good action rather than a single moment of change.
Shows anger stilled and the tablets retaken as guidance and mercy after the crisis.
Adds delayed reckoning: forgiveness and mercy do not erase accountability but postpone closure.
Names forgiveness and mercy amid gratitude, without adding a recovery condition.
Its death-and-revival parallel only indirectly accompanies the forgiveness horizon.
Distinguishes preventive guarding from forgiveness after failure.
Uses an after-clause for a separate interpersonal limit.
States the immediate consequence of taking the calf, defining the wrongdoing addressed by the focus.
Offers only a distant after-sequence of replacement and reverent fear.
Holds swift recompense with forgiveness and mercy while describing entrusted capacity as a test.
Adds judgment by each community's book, but repeats the record horizon already supplied.
Expands forgiveness into repentance, faith, righteous action, and continued guidance.
Offers an after-sequence of replacing a wrongful town, not personal recovery.
Sets broad mercy alongside specified responsive qualities, extending the focus's mercy and faith relation.
Only indirectly sharpens faith as a real trust relation.
Adds renewed faith, guarding, light, forgiveness, and mercy as an ongoing guided course.
The planked vessel parallel does not clarify repentance, faith, or forgiveness in the focus.
Supplies the contrary case: deeds lose weight when signs and final meeting are denied.
Connects faith and strenuous action with hope for mercy, but not the focus's wrongdoing-to-recovery movement.
Carries the surrounding passage into faithful following and release of burdens.
Provision and safety from hunger and fear do not clarify the focus.
Adds intercession for those who repent and follow the way, making mercy communal and directional.
The vessel's movement under care is not pertinent to the focus recovery reading.
Directly summons repentance and seeking forgiveness, but adds little beyond earlier parallels.
Adds repair, holding fast, and sincerity to repentance as restored belonging among believers.
Extends the local sequence into a call to faith, following, and guidance.
Distinguishes a promised later plea for forgiveness from immediate dismissal of fault.
Supplies punishment for plotting evil but no recovery route.
A dispute over the reminder in an unrelated vessel channel adds nothing to the focus.
Boundary evidence: association can nullify deeds, underscoring the stakes of believing reorientation.
Joins answering the call and believing with forgiveness and protection from punishment.
Its creation and gratitude scene does not materially clarify the focus.
Makes seeking forgiveness an imperative, with the speaker's own susceptibility to error in context.
Adds visible communal criteria after repentance before release, alongside forgiveness and mercy.
The verdict on an unrelated claimant contributes no recovery evidence.
The incapacity of other gods to avert harm does not clarify the focus sequence.
Supplies the contrary reckoning in which deeds become scattered, reinforcing why belief and repair matter.
Its association scene lacks a recovery or mercy connection to the focus.
Adds broad angelic seeking of forgiveness, but no distinct focus condition.
Provides a concrete corrective relation: good deeds remove evil deeds.
The warning of a whitening day does not clarify repentance or mercy here.
Holds forgiveness during wrongdoing with severe punishment, leaving an interval before final consequence.
Provides the contrary outcome for those who persist in earning evil deeds.
An isolated facial reaction in an unrelated channel has no interpretive value here.
Links requested mercy with prepared right guidance, but not recovery from evil.
Adds fine-grained accountability: every person has degrees corresponding to what was done.
The scorching description and its auxiliary board readings do not clarify the focus.
Contrasts proper post-hardship response with claiming mercy as personal entitlement.
Shows good action carrying good speech, sharpening the focus's faith as lived conduct.
Adds increase of faith through testing, but no direct recovery or mercy relation.
Shows habitual seeking of forgiveness, though it adds little beyond the established pattern.
Calls for believing in the sent confirmation, remotely supporting the focus's faith element.
Names active mercy as a source, but supplies no recovery sequence.
Adds disclosure of what people did at judgment, repeating the accountability horizon.
Connects faith and righteous action with release from fear and grief.
Parallels repentance plus public repair followed by forgiveness and mercy.
Connects believing righteous action with high degrees, without addressing prior evil.
Closely parallels wrongdoing, later repentance and repair, then divine turning and mercy.
Names the forgiving, merciful source as host, without a distinct recovery condition.
Adds a temporal boundary: repentance before capture opens the forgiveness horizon.
Questions belief after divine signs, a distant boundary on the focus's faith.
Adds seeking forgiveness followed by return, with mercy characterized by affection.
Joins repentance, faith, and righteous action with a protected favorable outcome.
Near-parallel: evil done in ignorance, later repentance and repair, under prescribed mercy and forgiveness.
Pairs the request for forgiveness with mercy as two needed forms of divine care.
Adds the strongest transformation claim: repentance, faith, and righteous action can turn evil deeds into good deeds.
Shows divergent responses to a given sign, only indirectly clarifying the faith condition.
Adds communal seeking of forgiveness in a ritual movement, but no distinct recovery mechanism.
Keeps punishment unsafe, a general boundary to presumptive confidence.
Warns against slipping after clear proofs, but does not articulate return or mercy.
Broadens mercy through the messenger's public sending, beyond the focus's personal recovery.
Warns against reversal into loss through following disbelievers; it only loosely bears on persevering faith.
Links Moses' book with guidance and mercy after earlier destruction, a distant narrative parallel.
The final endpoint belongs to the Lord, with no focused recovery contribution.
Names the Merciful and Compassionate frame but adds no condition or process.
Genealogical succession does not clarify the focus.
Joins guidance and mercy for believers, but remains a general restatement.
Condemns those staying behind in heat, without a recovery connection.
Shows righteous action rewarded in a special address, but not restoration after evil.
Adds repentance, repair, and open clarification as a route to divine turning and mercy.
Frames return in repentance as a positively received, continuing disposition.
Adds remembrance, seeking forgiveness, and refusal to persist after wrongdoing.
Adds observable repentance and repair as grounds for ending a punitive response.
Near-parallel wrongdoing in ignorance followed by timely repentance and divine acceptance.
Boundary evidence: repentance deferred until death is excluded from the open recovery interval.
Adds the removal of lesser evil deeds within a broader moral threshold.
Shows wrongdoers seeking forgiveness and receiving it through a merciful, accepting return.
Near-parallel: committing evil or self-wrong, then seeking forgiveness, meets the Forgiving, Merciful.
Boundary evidence: repeated reversal from belief blocks forgiveness and guidance.
Links belief and guarding with the covering of evil deeds and a favorable outcome.
Supplies a direct post-wrong plea for forgiveness and mercy, with loss as the contrary outcome.
Adds a commanded act of seeking release linked with forgiveness of wrongs.
Shows guarding as a means by which evil deeds are covered and forgiveness is granted.
Makes seeking forgiveness a condition that holds punishment at bay.
Names mixed good and evil deeds while leaving open divine acceptance of repentance.
States that divine acceptance of repentance and taking of restorative giving belongs to God.
Shows divine turning toward those who were left behind, after constriction and return.
Records belief only at overwhelming peril, setting the context for the following boundary.
Boundary evidence: a late declaration after prior disobedience is challenged rather than simply received.
Pairs seeking forgiveness with turning back in a continuing route of restored provision.
Forbids despair of divine relief, preserving hope around the focus's mercy horizon.
Adds reconciliation after grave wrong, including a prayer that forgiveness be granted.
Connects inward rectitude and repeated return with a forgiving response.
Joins belief with a request that prior sins and coercive wrongdoing be forgiven.
Names divine acceptance of repentance as the alternative to severe exposure.
Adds interpersonal pardon and overlooking under the pattern of seeking divine forgiveness.
Supplies grave wrongful acts as the antecedent for the repentance exception later in the passage.
States the intensified consequence that the following repentance, faith, and righteous action interrupt.
Directly asks why forgiveness is not sought before the demand for evil consequence.
Shows self-acknowledged wrong followed by a request for forgiveness and immediate forgiveness.
Links faith and righteous deeds with the covering of evil deeds.
Keeps divine turning toward a group open alongside accountability for another group.
Holds punishment and possible repentance together in the final division of responses.
Explicitly forbids despair after excess in wrongdoing and declares the breadth of forgiveness and mercy.
Commands turning and surrender before punishment, defining the open interval's urgency.
Names forgiveness of sin and acceptance of repentance while retaining severe punishment.
States acceptance of repentance and pardoning of evil deeds with knowledge of what is done.
Links affliction to what hands earned while affirming that much is pardoned.
Calls backbiting a violation and immediately opens repentance through divine acceptance and mercy.
Places forgiveness within a believing community's prayer for itself and those before it.
Holds former enmity, possible reconciliation, and divine forgiveness and mercy together.
Adds a covenantal renunciation of major wrongs followed by an instructed request for forgiveness.
Links faith and righteous action with the covering of evil deeds and entry into a favorable outcome.
Connects guarding with removal of evil deeds and enlargement of reward.
Commands a sincere repentance characterized by its capacity to cover evil deeds and admit into a favorable outcome.
Pairs unseen reverence with forgiveness and reward, supporting the focus's faith horizon.
Directly commands seeking forgiveness from the Forgiving source.
Closes a demanding passage by commanding the seeking of forgiveness and naming divine forgiveness and mercy.
Boundary evidence: harming believers remains punishable when it is not followed by repentance.
